title: Music & Rhythm
description: Music and rhythm from clapping games to composition: steady beat, loud and soft, high and low; instruments of India and the world; rhythm patterns and tala; melody and raga; reading notation; the Hindustani and Carnatic traditions alongside Western music; harmony, form and composing; and the science and cultural meaning of music.

lessons.title: Clap the Beat
objectives: Clap or tap a steady beat to a song
Tell the difference between fast and slow music
explanation: Most music has a steady beat, like a heartbeat or a clock ticking. We can clap, tap or march to the beat.
Some music has a fast beat that makes us want to run and jump. Some has a slow beat that makes us want to sway or rest. How fast or slow music goes is called tempo.
Our bodies are instruments too! We can clap, stamp, pat our knees and click our fingers. This is called body percussion.

vocabulary.meaning: how fast or slow music is

examples: Marching to a band.
Swaying slowly to a lullaby.

lessons.title: Loud and Soft, High and Low
objectives: Sing and play loudly and softly
Tell high sounds from low sounds
explanation: Sounds can be loud like a drum or soft like a whisper. In music, how loud or soft we play is called dynamics.
Sounds can also be high like a bird's tweet or low like a lion's roar. How high or low a sound is, is called pitch.
Small things often make higher sounds, and big things often make lower sounds — a small bell rings high, a big drum booms low.

vocabulary.meaning: how high or low a sound is
how loud or soft music is

A tiny flute and a big tuba.

lessons.title: How Instruments Make Sound
objectives: Sort instruments into strings, wind and percussion
Name Indian and world instruments in each family
explanation: Instruments make sound by making something vibrate (shake very fast). String instruments have strings that are plucked, bowed or struck: the sitar, veena, violin and guitar.
Wind instruments make sound when you blow air through them: the bansuri (bamboo flute), shehnai, trumpet and flute.
Percussion instruments are hit, shaken or scraped: the tabla, dholak, mridangam, drums, cymbals and the ghatam (a clay pot!).

vocabulary.meaning: instruments you hit, shake or scrape

examples: Plucking a sitar's strings.
Tapping a tabla.

story.title: The Instrument Parade
story.text: At the music festival, Zuri watched a parade. First came the strings: a sitar player plucking twinkly notes. Then the winds: a shehnai player puffing his cheeks. Last came the percussion: dhol drummers BOOM-BOOMING. "Every family sounds different," Zuri said, "but together they make a band!"

lessons.title: Ta, Ti-Ti and Rest
objectives: Clap long and short sounds in a pattern
Copy and create simple rhythm patterns
explanation: Rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds in music. The beat stays steady, but the rhythm changes.
We can use rhythm words: "ta" for one sound on a beat, "ti-ti" for two quick sounds on a beat, and "shh" for a rest (silence).
In Indian music, drummers learn rhythms by speaking syllables called bols, like "dha, dhin, na". Saying a rhythm helps us remember it.

vocabulary.meaning: a pattern of long and short sounds
a spoken drum syllable in Indian music

examples: Clapping "ta ta ti-ti ta".
A tabla player saying "dha dhin dhin dha".

story.title: Echo Mountain
story.text: On Echo Mountain, Ivaan clapped "ta, ta, ti-ti, ta". From across the valley came back: "ta, ta, ti-ti, ta!" He clapped a harder one with a rest: "ti-ti, ta, shh, ta." Back it came perfectly. "The mountain is a good listener," he laughed. "Or maybe it's my sister hiding behind the rock!"

lessons.title: Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni
objectives: Sing the sargam and solfège scales
Describe a melody as moving up, down or staying the same
explanation: A melody is a tune — a series of notes that go up, down or stay the same. A scale is a set of notes going up or down in order.

In Indian music, the seven notes (swaras) are Sa, Re, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni — called the sargam. In Western music, the notes are often sung Do, Re, Mi, Fa, So, La, Ti (solfège), or named C, D, E, F, G, A, B.
After Ni (or Ti), the scale returns to a higher Sa (or Do) — the same note, but higher. This is called an octave.

vocabulary.meaning: notes going up or down in order
the distance from one note to the same note higher or lower

examples: Singing Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni Sa.
"Do-Re-Mi" from a famous song.

story.title: The Musical Staircase
story.text: Ivaan's music teacher drew a staircase on the board with seven steps. "Sa" was on the bottom step. As Ivaan sang Re, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni, he climbed each step with his hand. At the top was another Sa, high and bright. "It's like the same friend, but standing on a chair!" Ivaan said.

lessons.title: Reading Notes
objectives: Read and clap note values: whole, half, quarter and eighth notes
Identify notes on the staff
explanation: Music can be written down so others can play it. In Western notation, a quarter note gets one beat, a half note gets two beats, a whole note gets four beats, and two eighth notes share one beat.
Notes are written on a staff — five lines and four spaces. The higher a note sits, the higher its pitch. A treble clef at the start shows higher notes.

Indian music has its own notation systems, such as the Bhatkhande system for Hindustani music, which writes swaras using letters. But much Indian music has traditionally been learned by ear from a guru.

vocabulary.meaning: five lines on which notes are written
a symbol that shows the pitch range of the staff

examples: Two half notes filling a bar of four beats.
Learning a raga by listening to a guru.

story.title: The Secret Code
story.text: Zuri found an old sheet of paper covered in dots and lines in her grandfather's cupboard. "It's a secret code!" she said. Her grandfather laughed and played it on his harmonium — it was his favourite song from when he was a boy. "Music writing lets songs travel through time," he said.

lessons.title: Melody Moods and Rhythm Cycles
objectives: Explain what a raga and a tala are
Count a tala cycle with claps and waves
explanation: A raga is a melodic framework: a set of notes with rules for how to move up (aroha) and down (avaroha), characteristic phrases and a mood (rasa). Many ragas are traditionally linked to times of day or seasons — Raga Bhairav to the morning, Raga Yaman to the evening.

A tala is a rhythmic cycle that repeats. Teentaal, common in Hindustani music, has 16 beats divided into four sections of four. The first beat, called sam, is the most important — musicians often meet there with a flourish.
In Carnatic music, Adi tala has 8 beats. Musicians keep tala with claps, finger counts and waves of the hand.

vocabulary.meaning: a melodic framework with rules and mood
the first and most important beat of a tala
the ascending pattern of a raga

examples: Raga Yaman sung in the evening.
A tabla player landing on sam with a smile.

story.title: Meeting at Sam
story.text: At a concert, Ivaan watched the sitar player and the tabla player improvise for many minutes. Their patterns grew wilder and more complex. Then, together, they landed on the first beat — DHA! — and the audience burst into "Wah!" "That's sam," his father whispered. "They planned to meet there all along."

lessons.title: Two Rivers of Music
objectives: Compare the Hindustani and Carnatic traditions
Describe the contributions of great musicians
explanation: Indian classical music has two main traditions. Hindustani music, mainly from North India, uses instruments like the sitar, sarod, tabla and bansuri, and forms such as khayal and dhrupad. It was shaped by both Hindu and Persian influences in royal courts.

Carnatic music, mainly from South India, uses the veena, violin, mridangam and ghatam. It is largely based on compositions (kritis); the "Trinity" of Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri composed many in the 18th–19th centuries.
Great musicians include Bharat Ratna awardees Pandit Ravi Shankar (sitar), M. S. Subbulakshmi (Carnatic vocal), Ustad Bismillah Khan (shehnai) and Pandit Bhimsen Joshi (Hindustani vocal).

vocabulary.meaning: a family or school of Hindustani music

examples: A khayal performance by a vocalist of the Kirana gharana.
A Tyagaraja kriti sung at a Carnatic concert.

story.title: Music at the Ganga
story.text: Every morning for decades, Ustad Bismillah Khan played his shehnai near the ghats of Varanasi. People said the river itself seemed to listen. In 1947, he played at the Red Fort on the eve of India's independence. In 2001 he received the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honour.

lessons.title: Major, Minor and the Drone
objectives: Build major and minor chords
Compare Western harmony with the Indian drone
prerequisites: Can read the staff and scales
explanation: Harmony is when different notes sound together. A chord is three or more notes played at once. A major chord (C–E–G) often sounds bright; a minor chord (C–E♭–G) often sounds darker or sadder — though such feelings are partly learned through culture.
Western music developed complex harmony, with chord progressions such as I–IV–V–I that underlie many songs.

Indian classical music focuses on melody over a drone — a continuous note (often Sa and Pa) played by the tanpura. Instead of changing chords, the melody explores the raga against this steady background.

vocabulary.meaning: three or more notes played at once

examples: A guitar strumming C, F and G chords.
The tanpura humming behind a vocalist.

story.title: The Tanpura's Hum
story.text: Before her concert, the singer tuned her tanpura until its four strings shimmered together in a soft, endless hum. "Why no chords?" asked a Western visitor. "The tanpura is the sky," she smiled, "and my voice is the bird. The sky doesn't need to change for the bird to fly."

lessons.title: The Shape of a Piece
objectives: Analyse common musical forms
Compose an original piece with clear form
explanation: Form is the structure of a piece. Many songs use verse–chorus form: verses tell the story with changing words; the chorus repeats. Other forms include ABA (ternary) and rondo (ABACA).
A Hindustani instrumental raga performance often follows alap (slow, free exploration without rhythm), jor (adding pulse), jhala (fast, exciting) and then a composition (gat) with tabla.
Composers plan contrast and repetition. Repetition helps listeners remember; contrast keeps them interested.

vocabulary.meaning: the structure of a piece of music
the repeated section of a song
the slow opening of a raga performance

examples: A pop song: verse, chorus, verse, chorus, bridge, chorus.
A sitar recital beginning with a long alap.

story.title: The Song That Wouldn't Leave
story.text: Kiko wrote a song with five verses and no chorus. His friends forgot it immediately. Then he added a catchy chorus between each verse. The next day, the whole class was humming it. "Repetition is a hook," his teacher said, "and contrast is the journey."

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Frequency, Harmonics and Tuning
objectives: Relate frequency to pitch and explain harmonics
Compare tuning systems
explanation: Sound is a vibration travelling through air. Its frequency (vibrations per second, measured in hertz, Hz) determines pitch. The note A above middle C is commonly tuned to 440 Hz; doubling the frequency gives the octave above (880 Hz).

Most instruments produce a fundamental frequency plus harmonics (overtones) at whole-number multiples. The mix of harmonics gives each instrument its timbre — why a sitar and a flute sound different on the same note. The sitar's jawari bridge creates a buzzing richness of overtones.

Tuning systems vary. Western music mostly uses 12-tone equal temperament, dividing the octave into 12 equal semitones. Indian music uses just intonation based on natural ratios, and theory describes 22 shrutis (microtones) in the octave.

vocabulary.meaning: the tone colour of a sound
a microtonal interval in Indian music theory

examples: A guitar string vibrating at 110 Hz for low A.
The tanpura's buzzing jawari.

story.title: Pythagoras and the Blacksmith
story.text: An old legend says Pythagoras heard hammers in a blacksmith's shop ringing in harmony and discovered that pleasing intervals came from simple ratios like 2:1 and 3:2. Historians doubt the story — hammers don't work that way — but the ratios themselves were really studied by Greek and Indian thinkers alike.

lessons.title: Why Humans Make Music
objectives: Evaluate theories about music's origins and effects
Analyse music's roles in identity and social movements
explanation: Every known human culture makes music. Scientists debate why: theories include social bonding, communication between parents and infants, and courtship. Brain imaging shows music activates areas for emotion, movement and memory; music therapy is used to help people with conditions such as stroke and dementia.
Music expresses identity — national anthems, devotional songs, regional folk music. "Jana Gana Mana", written by Rabindranath Tagore, was adopted as India's national anthem in 1950.
Music has powered social movements: "Vande Mataram" in India's freedom struggle, "We Shall Overcome" in the US civil rights movement, and songs against apartheid in South Africa.

vocabulary.meaning: a song representing a group or nation
a sense of who you are and belong with
mental processes such as thinking and memory

examples: Singing together at a festival.
Protest songs at marches.

story.title: The Song in the Hospital
story.text: A man who had lost his speech after a stroke could not say "good morning". But when a music therapist began a familiar song, he sang along, word for word. Researchers think singing uses brain networks partly different from speech — one reason music therapy can help.
